name: Kwaya
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Kwaya (kway1241) is not in the catalog. All seven swept titles concern Ci-Ruri, which Glottolog treats as a dialect of Kwaya (ruri1238 under kway1241; verified on glottolog.org). None of the seven could be read open: Massamba 1982 PhD (ProQuest preview only, priority high), Botne 1991 JALL (De Gruyter paywall, Crossref has no abstract; three duplicate Glottolog records; medium), Philippson 1991/92 thèse (theses.fr: not online; abstract read: East African Bantu systems range from pure tone to 'purely demarcative penultimate stress', with penultimate accent emergence as the diachronic driver; medium), Massamba 1992 JAAS 43 (CiNii record confirmed, no repository copy, TUFS repository unreachable; medium), Massamba 2005 OPiL (no online trace; low)., archive.org opensource scan, saved) pp. 235-238 -- Ci-Ruri is an accent language; accented verb stems carry the underlying accent on the stem-initial syllable; accent is realized as H on the next syllable, as H on the penult (penultimate back-hopping), or as a rise-fall on the last two syllables phrase-finally; (b) verified on file: Sillery 1932 p. 286 'The stress in Kikwaya is usually on the penultimate'; Goldsmith 1986 p. 96 'only one metrically strong position is established--the penultimate syllable' (page image read); Goldsmith's handout p. 2 restating Massamba 1982's accent-realization rules. Odom 2016 SIL orthography/grammar (on file) contain no stress statement (acute marks tone). Net: Kwaya/Ruri is a Bantu tone/pitch-accent language with penultimate prominence; the best explicit stress statement is Sillery 1932 (penultimate), and Massamba 1984 is the authoritative first-hand accent account.

Nothing on tone anywhere i…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable (author hedges with 'usually'; examples mark the penult with an acute). Modern SIL description (Odom 2016) shows Kwaya is a tone language (lexical LL/LH melodies, grammatical tone) but is silent on stress; for the Ruri dialect Goldsmith 1986:96 independently identifies the word-penult as the single metrically strong position (H tones shift rightward except off the penult).
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'usually'; no exceptions listed. (Goldsmith 1986 for Ruri: phrase-final H realized as rise-fall over the last two syllables.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms; Sillery gives isolated words. Goldsmith's Ruri statement is explicitly about the word ('not just of a phrase, but of any word') within a phrase-level tone-shift rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Sillery 1932 describes 'Kikwaya' of the Bakwaya on the Lake Victoria shore north of Musoma = Kwaya proper (kway1241, ISO kya). The modern prosodic literature (Massamba 1982/1984, Goldsmith 1986, Botne 1991) describes Ci-Ruri = Ruri, which Glottolog 5.1 lists as the sole dialect of Kwaya (ruri1238 under kway1241); SIL (Odom 2016) treats Ruri as a separate neighbouring language with 89% lexical similarity to Kwaya. The Goldsmith penult-prominence statement therefore applies to ruri1238 specifically.

new_statements.quote: 3. The stress in Kikwaya is usually on the penultimate : E.g. asokeréo, ntamenyére, Bakwáya.
new_statements.citation: Sillery, Anthony (1932). A sketch of the Kikwaya language. Bantu Studies 6: 273-308.
new_statements.reading: The only explicit word-stress statement for Kwaya proper: stress usually on the penultimate syllable (fixed penultimate, with 'usually' hedging). It is a brief 1932 sketch without tone analysis. The authoritative first-hand account of the Ruri dialect (Massamba 1984, pp. 235-238, fetched sources and read) instead analyses Ci-Ruri as a lexical pitch-accent language (stem-initial underlying accent on accented verb stems, realized as High on the following syllable / the penult / a phrase-final rise-fall), and Goldsmith 1986 p. 96 treats the penult as the sole metrically strong position; so a catalog entry should code Kwaya as a Bantu tone/accent language with penultimate prominence (Sillery) rather than a plain stress language.

sources.citation: Goldsmith, John (1986). Tone in the CiRuri present continuous. In K. Bogers, H. van der Hulst & M. Mous (eds.), The Phonological Representation of Suprasegmentals, 95-107. Dordrecht: Foris. [extra item]
sources.quote: CiRuri is a tone language of the Lacustrine area ... The most pervasive and unmistakable rule of CiRuri is a phrase-level rule that shifts all High tones one syllable to the right ... However, a High tone on the penultimate vowel of a word (not just of a phrase, but of any word) is not shifted; rather, it remains in place ... in CiRuri only one metrical foot is established per word, and only one metrically strong position is established--the penultimate syllable. All tones in a metrically weak position shift to the right by one syllable; a tone on the strong position does not shift.
sources.note: Ruri dialect, p. 96: CiRuri is a tone language; phrase-level rule shifts every H one syllable right, but an H on the penultimate vowel of any word does not shift; 'in CiRuri only one metrical foot is established per [word], and only one metrically strong position is established--the penultimate [syl]lable. All tones in a metrically weak position shift to the right by one [syl]lable; a tone on the strong position does not shift.' Data second-hand from Massamba 1982/1984.

sources.citation: Massamba, David P. B. (1984). Tone in Ci-Ruri. In G. N. Clements & John Goldsmith (eds.), Autosegmental Studies in Bantu Tone, 235-254. Dordrecht: Foris. doi 10.1515/9783110864465.235 [extra item, not in the title sweep; the published digest of Massamba 1982]
sources.quote: The present discussion is based on the premise that Ci-Ruri, a Bantu language spoken in Tanzania, is an accent language, and that the tones which are exhibited in this language are surface manifestations of an underlying accent system. [p. 235] ... If an accent falls on an antepenultimate syllable or earlier in a word, it is realized as a High on the immediately following syllable ... If it falls on the penultimate syllable, it will first hop back to the immediately preceding syllable ... a High appears on the penult. [p. 237] ... in Ci-Ruri, as in many other Bantu languages, all accented verb stems have their underlying accent on the first syllable of the stem, although the accent can be realized tonally elsewhere. [p. 238]
sources.note: First-hand (native-speaker linguist). Ci-Ruri (Ruri dialect of Kwaya) is analysed as a lexical pitch-accent language: verb stems are lexically accented or unaccented; accented stems carry the accent on the stem-initial syllable; the accent is realized as a High tone on the following syllable (or on the penult, via penultimate back-hopping, or as a Rise-Fall on the last two syllables when phrase-final). This is an accent/tone system, not a stress system; no statement of a fixed word-stress position.

sources.citation: Goldsmith, John (n.d.). Tone and Accent in Bantu (handout; section 'RURI (Ci-Ruri) Source: Massamba 1982'). [extra item; second-hand digest of Massamba 1982]
sources.quote: RURI (Ci-Ruri) Source: Massamba 1982. Accent Realization: 1. An accent on a phrase-final vowel is realized as a Rise-Fall over the last two vowels. 2. An accent on the penultimate syllable of a word is realized as a High tone on that vowel. 3. Elsewhere, an accent is realized as a High tone on the following syllable.
sources.note: Second-hand summary of the unread 1982 thesis; matches Massamba 1984 sec. 4 (read).

sources.citation: Goldsmith, John. n.d. Tone and Accent in Bantu (handout, author's website).
sources.note: Ci-Ruri (source Massamba 1982) accent-realization rules: accent on phrase-final vowel = rise-fall over last two vowels; accent on word-penult = H on that vowel; elsewhere accent = H on following vowel. Handout, not a publication.

sources.quote: We find at one end purely tonal systems (like kikuyu) and at the other end systems with purely demarcative penultimate stress, with all intermediate cases. ... a hypothesis is presented according to which the emergence of penultimate accent is the main cause of the evolution of these systems.
sources.note: Abstract (theses.fr, read): 'This work studies the very diverse prosodic systems of east African bantu languages... We find at one end purely tonal systems (like kikuyu) and at the other end systems with purely demarcative penultimate stress, with all intermediate cases... a hypothesis is presented according to which the emergence of penultimate accent is the main cause of the evolution of these systems.' Comparative over ~30 languages; whether Ruri/Kwaya is one of them is not stated in the abstract (Glottolog links it to kway1241). Print only (Paris 5).
